Does spending more time browsing products have a different association with purchase likelihood for new versus returning online shoppers, after accounting for other browsing behaviors and session characteristics?

# A. Data Preparation and Exploratory Data Analysis

## 1 Data Import

```{r}
# Load packages used for data preparation, summaries, and visualization
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(moments)
library(corrplot)

# Import the online shoppers dataset
df <- read_csv("data/online_shoppers_intention.csv")

# Inspect the dataset dimensions, object class, and variable structure
dim(df)
class(df)
glimpse(df)
```

## 2 Data Quality Assessment

### 2.1 Missing Values

```{r}
sum(is.na(df))
colSums(is.na(df))
```

No missing values were identified in the dataset.

### 2.2 Duplicate Records

```{r}
sum(duplicated(df))
mean(duplicated(df)) * 100

df[duplicated(df), ] %>%
  count(Revenue)
```

A total of 125 duplicate records (1.01% of the dataset) were identified, all corresponding to non-purchasing sessions. Since the dataset does not contain unique session identifiers, these records were retained provisionally because identical observations may represent distinct browsing sessions.

### 2.3 Data Types and Summary

```{r}
sapply(df, class)
summary(df)
```

```{r}
df %>%
  select(Month, OperatingSystems, Browser, Region,
         TrafficType, VisitorType, Weekend, Revenue) %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), n_distinct))
```

## 3 Unusual Observations

### 3.1 Invalid Values

```{r}
df %>%
  summarise(
    # Count observations with negative page counts
    negative_counts = sum(
      Administrative < 0 |
        Informational < 0 |
        ProductRelated < 0
    ),
    
    # Count observations with negative browsing durations
    negative_durations = sum(
      Administrative_Duration < 0 |
        Informational_Duration < 0 |
        ProductRelated_Duration < 0
    ),
    
    # Check if bounce rates fall outside the range [0, 1]
    invalid_bounce_rates = sum(
      BounceRates < 0 | BounceRates > 1
    ),
    
    # Check if exit rates fall outside the range [0, 1]
    invalid_exit_rates = sum(
      ExitRates < 0 | ExitRates > 1
    ),
    
    # Check if SpecialDay values fall outside the range [0, 1]
    invalid_special_day = sum(
      SpecialDay < 0 | SpecialDay > 1
    )
  )
```

No negative page counts, negative browsing durations, or values outside the valid ranges for bounce rate, exit rate, or special-day proximity were identified.

### 3.2 Zero Browsing Duration

```{r}
df %>%
  summarise(
    # Count sessions with zero product browsing duration
    zero_duration = sum(ProductRelated_Duration == 0),
    
    # Count sessions with no product page visits
    zero_pages = sum(ProductRelated == 0),
    
    # Count sessions with page visits but no recorded duration
    zero_duration_with_pages = sum(
      ProductRelated_Duration == 0 & ProductRelated > 0
    ),
    
    # Count sessions with recorded duration but no page visits
    duration_without_pages = sum(
      ProductRelated_Duration > 0 & ProductRelated == 0
    )
  )
```

A total of 755 sessions had zero product browsing duration, including 717 sessions that visited at least one product-related page. This may reflect the way browsing time was recorded rather than data errors. Therefore, these observations were retained provisionally.

### 3.3 Outlier Detection

```{r}
# Calculate the 25th and 75th percentiles
q1 <- quantile(df$ProductRelated_Duration, 0.25)
q3 <- quantile(df$ProductRelated_Duration, 0.75)

# Calculate the interquartile range
iqr <- q3 - q1

# Define outlier thresholds using the 1.5 IQR rule
lower_bound <- q1 - 1.5 * iqr
upper_bound <- q3 + 1.5 * iqr

# Display the lower and upper thresholds
lower_bound
upper_bound

# Count observations outside the defined thresholds
sum(df$ProductRelated_Duration < lower_bound |
      df$ProductRelated_Duration > upper_bound)
```

Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, 961 observations were identified as potential outliers in product browsing duration. The lower and upper bounds were −1,735.89 and 3,384.19 seconds, respectively. These observations were retained provisionally because unusually long browsing durations do not necessarily indicate data errors.

### 3.4 Product Browsing Duration Boxplot

```{r}
#| label: fig-duration-boxplot
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of product browsing duration, including potential outliers."

# Set product browsing duration as the y-axis variable
ggplot(df, aes(y = ProductRelated_Duration)) +
  
  # Create a boxplot to display the distribution and outliers
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  
  # Set the plot title and y-axis label
  labs(
    title = "Product Browsing Duration",
    y = "Duration (seconds)"
  ) +
  
  # Apply a minimal plot theme
  theme_minimal()
```

Product browsing duration exhibited a strongly right-skewed distribution with numerous extreme values. A logarithmic transformation was therefore explored to reduce skewness.

## 4 Duration Distribution and Transformation

### 4.1 Convert Duration to Minutes

```{r}
# Convert product browsing duration from seconds to minutes
df <- df %>%
  mutate(Duration_Minutes = ProductRelated_Duration / 60)

# Display descriptive statistics for browsing duration
summary(df$Duration_Minutes)

# Calculate the standard deviation
sd(df$Duration_Minutes)

# Calculate skewness of the original distribution
skewness(df$Duration_Minutes)
```

Product browsing duration was converted from seconds to minutes for easier interpretation. The average browsing duration was 19.91 minutes, with a median of 9.98 minutes and a standard deviation of 31.89 minutes.

### 4.2 Original Duration Distribution

```{r}
#| label: fig-original-duration
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of product browsing duration in minutes. The dashed line marks the median."

ggplot(df, aes(x = Duration_Minutes)) +
  
  # Divide browsing duration into 50 histogram bins
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue",
                 color = "white") +
  
  # Add a dashed line representing the median
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = median(df$Duration_Minutes),
    color = "red", linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  
  # Set the title and axis labels
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Product Browsing Duration",
    x = "Browsing Duration (minutes)",
    y = "Number of Sessions"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The original duration distribution was highly right-skewed, with a skewness of 7.262. Most sessions had relatively short browsing durations, while a small proportion had substantially longer durations.

### 4.3 Log Transformation

```{r}
# Apply log transformation while preserving zero values
df <- df %>%
  mutate(Log_Duration = log1p(Duration_Minutes))

# Display descriptive statistics after transformation
summary(df$Log_Duration)

# Calculate skewness after transformation
skewness(df$Log_Duration)
```

A log(1 + x) transformation was applied to reduce skewness and compress extreme values while preserving zero-duration observations.

### 4.4 Transformed Duration Distribution

```{r}
#| label: fig-log-duration
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of log-transformed product browsing duration. The dashed line marks the median."

ggplot(df, aes(x = Log_Duration)) +
  
  # Plot the distribution of log-transformed duration
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue",
                 color = "white") +
  
  # Add a dashed line representing the median
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = median(df$Log_Duration),
    color = "red", linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  
  # Set the title and axis labels
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Log-Transformed Browsing Duration",
    x = "Log(1 + Duration in Minutes)",
    y = "Number of Sessions"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The transformed distribution was substantially more symmetric, although a noticeable concentration of observations remained at zero.

### 4.5 Compare Skewness

```{r}
#| label: tbl-skewness-comparison

# Compare skewness before and after log transformation
skewness_table <- tibble(
  Variable = c("Original Duration", "Log Duration"),
  Skewness = c(
    skewness(df$Duration_Minutes),
    skewness(df$Log_Duration)
  )
)

# Display the comparison table
kable(skewness_table, digits = 3,
      caption = "Skewness Before and After Log Transformation")
```

The log transformation reduced skewness from 7.262 to −0.076. Both original and transformed durations were retained for subsequent model development. The final functional form should be determined through model diagnostics rather than predictor normality alone.

## 5 Data Cleaning and Variable Recoding

### 5.1 Examine Visitor Categories

```{r}
#| label: tbl-visitor-categories-before-restriction

visitor_category_summary <- df %>%
  # Group sessions by visitor type
  group_by(VisitorType) %>%
  
  summarise(
    # Count the total number of sessions
    Sessions = n(),
    
    # Count sessions resulting in a purchase
    Purchases = sum(Revenue),
    
    # Calculate the percentage of purchasing sessions
    Conversion_Rate = mean(Revenue) * 100,
    
    # Remove grouping after summarization
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Display the visitor categories with reader-friendly labels
kable(
  visitor_category_summary %>%
    mutate(
      VisitorType = recode(
        VisitorType,
        New_Visitor = "New Visitor",
        Returning_Visitor = "Returning Visitor"
      )
    ),
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c(
    "Visitor Type", "Sessions", "Purchases", "Conversion Rate (%)"
  ),
  caption = "Visitor Categories Before the Analytical Restriction"
)
```

The dataset contains three visitor categories: new visitors, returning visitors, and other visitors. The Other category contains only 85 observations, representing approximately 0.69% of the dataset. Since the research question focuses on new and returning visitors, the Other category is excluded from the proposed analytical dataset.

### 5.2 Create Analytical Dataset

```{r}
df_clean <- df %>%
  
  # Retain only new and returning visitors
  filter(VisitorType %in% c("New_Visitor", "Returning_Visitor")) %>%
  
  mutate(
    # Convert the binary outcome from TRUE/FALSE to 1/0
    Revenue = as.integer(Revenue),
    
    # Set new visitors as the reference category
    VisitorType = factor(
      VisitorType,
      levels = c("New_Visitor", "Returning_Visitor")
    ),
    
    # Convert numeric category codes into factors
    OperatingSystems = factor(OperatingSystems),
    Browser = factor(Browser),
    Region = factor(Region),
    TrafficType = factor(TrafficType),
    
    # Convert month into a categorical variable
    Month = factor(Month),
    
    # Convert weekend status into a binary factor
    Weekend = factor(Weekend, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE))
  )
```

The purchase outcome was recoded as a binary variable, with 1 representing a purchase and 0 representing no purchase. Visitor type was converted into a factor, with new visitors as the reference category. Other categorical variables were converted into factors to prevent their numerical codes from being interpreted as continuous measurements.

### 5.3 Verify the Cleaned Dataset

```{r}
# Check the number of observations and variables
dim(df_clean)

# Inspect the updated variable types
glimpse(df_clean)

# Verify the visitor type reference category
levels(df_clean$VisitorType)

# Check the distribution of the binary outcome
table(df_clean$Revenue)

# Check whether recoding introduced missing values
sum(is.na(df_clean))
```

The cleaned dataset contains 12,245 observations and 20 variables, including the original browsing duration, duration in minutes, and log-transformed duration. All variables were successfully recoded, and no missing values were introduced during data preparation.

### 5.4 Data Cleaning Summary

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cleaning-summary

# Create a summary of observations before and after cleaning
cleaning_summary <- tibble(
  Description = c(
    "Original dataset",
    "Excluded other visitors",
    "Final analytical dataset"
  ),
  
  # Calculate the corresponding observation counts
  Observations = c(
    nrow(df),
    nrow(df) - nrow(df_clean),
    nrow(df_clean)
  )
)

# Calculate each count as a percentage of the original dataset
cleaning_summary <- cleaning_summary %>%
  mutate(
    Percentage = Observations / nrow(df) * 100
  )

# Display the formatted cleaning summary table
kable(
  cleaning_summary,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Data Cleaning Summary"
)
```

A total of 85 observations were excluded based on the visitor type restriction. The resulting analytical dataset retained 99.31% of the original observations. No additional observations were removed solely because of duplicate values, zero browsing durations, or potential outliers.

### 5.5 Export Cleaned Dataset

```{r}
# Export the cleaned dataset as a CSV file
write_csv(
  df_clean,
  "data/online_shoppers_cleaned.csv"
)

# Save the R dataset while preserving factor levels and data types
saveRDS(
  df_clean,
  "data/online_shoppers_cleaned.rds"
)
```

## 6 Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

### 6.1 Descriptive Statistics

#### 6.1.1 Numerical Variables

```{r}
#| label: tbl-numerical-descriptive-statistics

descriptive_stats <- df_clean %>%
  
  # Select numerical variables relevant to the analysis
  select(
    Administrative,
    Administrative_Duration,
    Informational,
    Informational_Duration,
    ProductRelated,
    Duration_Minutes,
    Log_Duration,
    BounceRates,
    ExitRates,
    PageValues,
    SpecialDay
  ) %>%
  
  # Convert numerical variables into a long-format dataset
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "Variable",
    values_to = "Value"
  ) %>%
  
  # Group values by their original variable names
  group_by(Variable) %>%
  
  summarise(
    # Calculate measures of central tendency
    Mean = mean(Value),
    Median = median(Value),
    
    # Calculate standard deviation
    SD = sd(Value),
    
    # Calculate the first and third quartiles
    Q1 = quantile(Value, 0.25),
    Q3 = quantile(Value, 0.75),
    
    # Identify minimum and maximum values
    Min = min(Value),
    Max = max(Value),
    
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%

  # Replace code-style variable names with reader-friendly labels
  mutate(
    Variable = recode(
      Variable,
      Administrative = "Administrative Pages",
      Administrative_Duration = "Administrative Duration (seconds)",
      Informational = "Informational Pages",
      Informational_Duration = "Informational Duration (seconds)",
      ProductRelated = "Product Pages",
      Duration_Minutes = "Product Duration (minutes)",
      Log_Duration = "Log Product Duration",
      BounceRates = "Bounce Rate",
      ExitRates = "Exit Rate",
      PageValues = "Page Value",
      SpecialDay = "Special-Day Proximity"
    )
  )

# Display the formatted descriptive statistics table
kable(
  descriptive_stats,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Descriptive Statistics of Numerical Variables"
)
```

The average product browsing duration was 19.98 minutes, with a median of 10.04 minutes and a standard deviation of 31.95 minutes. The difference between the mean and median indicates a right-skewed distribution and substantial variation in product engagement across sessions.

#### 6.1.2 Categorical Variables

```{r}
#| label: tbl-categorical-descriptive-statistics

categorical_stats <- df_clean %>%
  
  # Select categorical variables of interest
  select(VisitorType, Weekend, Month, Revenue) %>%
  
  # Convert selected variables to character for reshaping
  mutate(across(everything(), as.character)) %>%
  
  # Reshape categorical variables into long format
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "Variable",
    values_to = "Category"
  ) %>%
  
  # Count observations within each category
  count(Variable, Category, name = "Frequency") %>%
  
  # Calculate percentages within each variable
  group_by(Variable) %>%
  mutate(
    Percentage = Frequency / sum(Frequency) * 100
  ) %>%
  
  # Remove grouping after calculation
  ungroup() %>%

  # Replace code-style values with reader-friendly display labels
  mutate(
    Variable = recode(
      Variable,
      VisitorType = "Visitor Type",
      Weekend = "Weekend Session",
      Month = "Month",
      Revenue = "Purchase Outcome"
    ),
    Category = recode(
      Category,
      New_Visitor = "New Visitor",
      Returning_Visitor = "Returning Visitor",
      `FALSE` = "No",
      `TRUE` = "Yes",
      `0` = "No Purchase",
      `1` = "Purchase"
    )
  )

# Display the categorical summary table
kable(
  categorical_stats,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Descriptive Statistics of Categorical Variables"
)
```

Returning visitors accounted for the majority of the analytical sample (86.16%), while new visitors represented 13.84%. This imbalance in visitor composition should be considered when interpreting subsequent comparisons between the two groups.

### 6.2 Purchase Outcome Distribution

#### 6.2.1 Calculate Purchase Distribution

```{r}
#| label: tbl-purchase-outcome-distribution

# Group sessions by purchase outcome and count observations
purchase_distribution <- df_clean %>%
  count(Revenue, name = "Sessions") %>%
  
  mutate(
    # Calculate the percentage of each purchase outcome
    Percentage = Sessions / sum(Sessions) * 100,
    
    # Replace numeric outcome codes with descriptive labels
    Purchase = factor(
      Revenue,
      levels = c(0, 1),
      labels = c("No Purchase", "Purchase")
    )
  )

# Display the purchase outcome summary
kable(
  purchase_distribution %>%
    select(Purchase, Sessions, Percentage),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Purchase Outcome Distribution"
)
```

#### 6.2.2 Visualize Purchase Distribution

```{r}
#| label: fig-purchase-outcome-distribution
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of purchase outcomes in the analytical sample."

ggplot(purchase_distribution,
       aes(x = Purchase, y = Percentage, fill = Purchase)) +
  
  # Create bars using the calculated percentages
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  
  # Display percentages above each bar
  geom_text(
    aes(label = sprintf("%.2f%%", Percentage)),
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 4
  ) +
  
  # Assign colors to the two purchase outcomes
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("steelblue", "seagreen")
  ) +
  
  # Set the percentage axis from 0 to 100
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 100),
    breaks = seq(0, 100, 20),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")
  ) +
  
  # Set the plot title and axis labels
  labs(
    title = "Purchase Outcome Distribution",
    x = "Purchase Outcome",
    y = "Percentage of Sessions"
  ) +
  
  # Apply a minimal theme and remove the redundant legend
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Among the 12,245 sessions, 1,892 (15.45%) resulted in a purchase, while 10,353 (84.55%) did not. This indicates a substantial class imbalance in the purchase outcome. Consequently, classification accuracy alone may be misleading when evaluating model performance.

### 6.3 Product Browsing Duration Distribution

#### 6.3.1 Prepare Distribution Data

```{r}
duration_distribution <- df_clean %>%
  
  # Select original and log-transformed browsing durations
  select(Duration_Minutes, Log_Duration) %>%
  
  # Reshape the data to compare both distributions
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "Transformation",
    values_to = "Duration"
  ) %>%
  
  # Assign descriptive labels to both distributions
  mutate(
    Transformation = factor(
      Transformation,
      levels = c("Duration_Minutes", "Log_Duration"),
      labels = c(
        "Original Duration (Minutes)",
        "Log-Transformed Duration"
      )
    )
  )
```

#### 6.3.2 Visualize Both Distributions

```{r}
#| label: fig-duration-transformation-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Product browsing duration before and after the log transformation. Panels use independent axis scales."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5

ggplot(duration_distribution, aes(x = Duration)) +
  
  # Create histograms for both duration measurements
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 50,
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  
  # Allow independent axis scales for both distributions
  facet_wrap(
    ~ Transformation,
    scales = "free",
    ncol = 2
  ) +
  
  # Set the title and axis labels
  labs(
    title = "Product Browsing Duration Before and After Transformation",
    x = "Browsing Duration",
    y = "Number of Sessions"
  ) +
  
  # Apply a consistent visual theme
  theme_minimal()
```

Product browsing duration was strongly right-skewed, with most sessions concentrated at shorter durations. The log transformation produced a substantially more symmetric distribution while preserving zero-duration sessions. Because the panels use independent axis scales, their bar heights should not be compared directly.

### 6.4 Conversion Rate by Visitor Type

#### 6.4.1 Calculate Conversion Rates

```{r}
#| label: tbl-conversion-rate-by-visitor-type

visitor_conversion <- df_clean %>%
  
  # Group sessions by visitor type
  group_by(VisitorType) %>%
  
  summarise(
    # Count total sessions within each visitor group
    Sessions = n(),
    
    # Count sessions resulting in a purchase
    Purchases = sum(Revenue),
    
    # Calculate the purchase conversion rate
    Conversion_Rate = mean(Revenue) * 100,
    
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  
  # Replace category codes with descriptive labels
  mutate(
    Visitor = factor(
      VisitorType,
      levels = c("New_Visitor", "Returning_Visitor"),
      labels = c("New Visitor", "Returning Visitor")
    )
  )

# Display the conversion rate summary table
kable(
  visitor_conversion %>%
    select(Visitor, Sessions, Purchases, Conversion_Rate),
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c(
    "Visitor Type", "Sessions", "Purchases", "Conversion Rate (%)"
  ),
  caption = "Purchase Conversion Rates by Visitor Type"
)
```

#### 6.4.2 Visualize Conversion Rates

```{r}
#| label: fig-conversion-rate-by-visitor-type
#| fig-cap: "Observed purchase conversion rates for new and returning visitors."

ggplot(visitor_conversion,
       aes(x = Visitor, y = Conversion_Rate, fill = Visitor)) +
  
  # Create bars representing group-specific conversion rates
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  
  # Display conversion percentages above each bar
  geom_text(
    aes(label = sprintf("%.2f%%", Conversion_Rate)),
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 4
  ) +
  
  # Assign distinct colors to visitor groups
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("steelblue", "seagreen")
  ) +
  
  # Format the y-axis as percentages
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%"),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))
  ) +
  
  # Set the title and axis labels
  labs(
    title = "Purchase Conversion Rate by Visitor Type",
    x = "Visitor Type",
    y = "Conversion Rate"
  ) +
  
  # Apply a minimal theme and remove the redundant legend
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

New visitors had a higher observed purchase conversion rate (24.91%) than returning visitors (13.93%), a difference of 10.98 percentage points. However, this unadjusted comparison does not account for differences in browsing behavior or other session characteristics.

### 6.5 Browsing Duration and Conversion by Visitor Type

#### 6.5.1 Create Duration Groups

```{r}
#| label: tbl-conversion-by-duration-and-visitor-type

duration_conversion <- df_clean %>%
  
  mutate(
    # Divide browsing duration into meaningful time intervals
    Duration_Group = cut(
      Duration_Minutes,
      breaks = c(0, 5, 10, 20, 30, 60, Inf),
      labels = c(
        "0-5 min",
        "5-10 min",
        "10-20 min",
        "20-30 min",
        "30-60 min",
        "60+ min"
      ),
      include.lowest = TRUE,
      right = FALSE
    )
  ) %>%
  
  # Group sessions by browsing duration and visitor type
  group_by(Duration_Group, VisitorType) %>%
  
  summarise(
    # Count sessions within each group
    Sessions = n(),
    
    # Count sessions resulting in purchases
    Purchases = sum(Revenue),
    
    # Calculate the purchase conversion rate
    Conversion_Rate = mean(Revenue) * 100,
    
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Display conversion rates across duration and visitor groups
kable(
  duration_conversion %>%
    mutate(
      VisitorType = recode(
        as.character(VisitorType),
        New_Visitor = "New Visitor",
        Returning_Visitor = "Returning Visitor"
      )
    ),
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c(
    "Duration Group", "Visitor Type", "Sessions",
    "Purchases", "Conversion Rate (%)"
  ),
  caption = "Purchase Conversion by Duration and Visitor Type"
)
```

#### 6.5.2 Visualize Duration and Conversion

```{r}
#| label: fig-conversion-by-duration-and-visitor-type
#| fig-cap: "Observed purchase conversion rates across browsing-duration groups for new and returning visitors."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

ggplot(
  duration_conversion,
  aes(
    x = Duration_Group,
    y = Conversion_Rate,
    color = VisitorType,
    group = VisitorType
  )
) +
  
  # Connect conversion rates across duration groups
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  
  # Display the observed conversion rate for each group
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  
  # Assign colors and descriptive labels to visitor types
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("steelblue", "seagreen"),
    labels = c("New Visitor", "Returning Visitor")
  ) +
  
  # Format the conversion rate axis as percentages
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%"),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.1))
  ) +
  
  # Set the plot title, axis labels, and legend title
  labs(
    title = "Purchase Conversion by Browsing Duration and Visitor Type",
    x = "Product Browsing Duration",
    y = "Conversion Rate",
    color = "Visitor Type"
  ) +
  
  # Apply a minimal theme and position the legend
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Purchase conversion rates generally increased with product browsing duration for both visitor types. New visitors consistently exhibited higher conversion rates than returning visitors across all duration groups. The difference between the two groups varied with browsing duration, suggesting a potential interaction between browsing duration and visitor type. However, the conversion rate for new visitors in the 60+ minute group should be interpreted cautiously due to the small sample size (n = 15). Further regression analysis is required to determine whether the interaction is statistically significant.

### 6.6 Relationships Between Potential Confounders

#### 6.6.1 Correlation Matrix

```{r}
# Select numerical predictors relevant to browsing behavior
correlation_data <- df_clean %>%
  select(
    Administrative,
    Administrative_Duration,
    Informational,
    Informational_Duration,
    ProductRelated,
    Duration_Minutes,
    BounceRates,
    ExitRates,
    SpecialDay
  )

# Calculate Pearson correlation coefficients
correlation_matrix <- cor(
  correlation_data,
  method = "pearson"
)

# Store correlation coefficients rounded to three decimals
# for concise reporting without printing a duplicate wide matrix
correlation_matrix_rounded <- round(correlation_matrix, 3)
```

#### 6.6.2 Visualize the Correlation Matrix

```{r}
#| label: fig-predictor-correlation-matrix
#| fig-cap: "Pearson correlations among selected numerical predictors."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7

# Create descriptive labels for numerical predictors
variable_labels <- c(
  "Administrative Pages",
  "Administrative Duration",
  "Informational Pages",
  "Informational Duration",
  "Product Pages",
  "Product Duration",
  "Bounce Rate",
  "Exit Rate",
  "Special Day"
)

# Replace variable names with descriptive labels
colnames(correlation_matrix) <- variable_labels
rownames(correlation_matrix) <- variable_labels

# Visualize correlations using a lower triangular heatmap
corrplot(
  correlation_matrix,
  method = "color",
  type = "lower",
  
  # Display correlation coefficients inside each cell
  addCoef.col = "black",
  number.cex = 0.55,
  
  # Format variable labels
  tl.col = "black",
  tl.srt = 45,
  tl.cex = 0.7,
  
  # Hide the diagonal self-correlations
  diag = FALSE,
  
  # Define colors for negative and positive correlations
  col = colorRampPalette(
    c("firebrick", "white", "steelblue")
  )(200),

  # Reduce outer margins so labels remain attached to the matrix
  mar = c(0, 0, 1, 0)
)
```

#### 6.6.3 Identify Highly Correlated Variables

```{r}
#| label: tbl-highly-correlated-predictors

# Identify strongly correlated variable pairs
high_correlations <- which(
  abs(correlation_matrix) >= 0.7 &
    upper.tri(correlation_matrix),
  arr.ind = TRUE
)

# Create a table of strongly correlated predictors
high_correlation_table <- tibble(
  
  # Extract the names of the first and second variables
  Variable_1 = rownames(correlation_matrix)[
    high_correlations[, 1]
  ],
  Variable_2 = colnames(correlation_matrix)[
    high_correlations[, 2]
  ],
  
  # Extract the corresponding correlation coefficients
  Correlation = correlation_matrix[high_correlations]
) %>%
  
  # Sort variable pairs by absolute correlation strength
  arrange(desc(abs(Correlation)))

# Display the formatted correlation table
kable(
  high_correlation_table,
  digits = 3,
  col.names = c("Variable 1", "Variable 2", "Correlation"),
  caption = "Highly Correlated Numerical Predictors"
)
```

The correlation analysis identified two strongly correlated predictor pairs: bounce rate and exit rate (r = 0.913), and product page count and product browsing duration (r = 0.861). Including both variables from either pair may introduce multicollinearity. These relationships should be considered during covariate selection and further assessed using variance inflation factors (VIF).

#### 6.6.4 Examine Categorical Session Characteristics

```{r}
#| label: tbl-session-characteristics-by-visitor-type

# Group sessions by visitor type
session_characteristics <- df_clean %>%
  group_by(VisitorType) %>%
  
  summarise(
    # Calculate the average product browsing duration
    Mean_Duration = mean(Duration_Minutes),
    
    # Calculate the median product browsing duration
    Median_Duration = median(Duration_Minutes),
    
    # Calculate the average number of product pages visited
    Mean_Product_Pages = mean(ProductRelated),
    
    # Calculate the percentage of weekend sessions
    Weekend_Percentage = mean(Weekend == "TRUE") * 100,
    
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Display browsing characteristics by visitor type
kable(
  session_characteristics %>%
    mutate(
      VisitorType = recode(
        as.character(VisitorType),
        New_Visitor = "New Visitor",
        Returning_Visitor = "Returning Visitor"
      )
    ),
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c(
    "Visitor Type", "Mean Duration (min)", "Median Duration (min)",
    "Mean Product Pages", "Weekend Sessions (%)"
  ),
  caption = "Session Characteristics by Visitor Type"
)
```

Returning visitors spent more time browsing product-related pages than new visitors, averaging 21.49 minutes compared with 10.61 minutes. They also visited more product-related pages per session (34.08 versus 18.05). Despite greater observed product engagement, returning visitors had a lower overall purchase conversion rate. These differences highlight the importance of accounting for browsing behaviors and session characteristics when examining purchase conversion.

## 7 Summary of EDA Findings

The final analytical dataset consisted of 12,245 browsing sessions, of which 15.45% resulted in a purchase. Returning visitors represented 86.17% of the sample.

Product browsing duration was highly right-skewed, and a log transformation substantially reduced skewness while preserving zero-duration observations.

New visitors exhibited a higher overall conversion rate than returning visitors (24.91% versus 13.93%), despite spending less time browsing product-related pages and visiting fewer product pages on average.

Purchase conversion rates generally increased with browsing duration for both visitor types. However, the difference in conversion rates varied across duration groups, suggesting that visitor type may modify the relationship between product engagement and purchase conversion. Estimates for new visitors in the longest duration group should be interpreted cautiously due to the small sample size.

The correlation analysis also identified strong relationships between bounce rate and exit rate (r = 0.913) and between product page count and browsing duration (r = 0.861), highlighting potential multicollinearity concerns.

These exploratory findings motivate a multiple logistic regression model incorporating an interaction between product browsing duration and visitor type while accounting for relevant browsing behaviors and session characteristics.

## 8 Report Contributions

### 8.1 Problem Motivation and Stakeholder Context

Understanding how online browsing behavior relates to purchase conversion is important for e-commerce businesses seeking to improve customer experience and sales performance. Online shoppers may abandon their shopping carts because they are browsing or comparing products rather than intending to make an immediate purchase (Holst, 2025).

Previous research has demonstrated the usefulness of browsing behavior in predicting online purchase intentions (Sakar et al., 2019). However, the relationship between product engagement and purchase conversion may differ between new and returning visitors.

This analysis is intended for e-commerce product managers seeking to understand customer behavior and identify opportunities for segment-specific website optimization.

### 8.2 Research Question

How does the relationship between engagement with product-related pages and the likelihood of completing an online purchase differ between new and returning visitors, after accounting for other browsing behaviors and session characteristics?

### 8.3 Key Descriptive Findings

Among the 12,245 browsing sessions analyzed, 15.45% resulted in a purchase. New visitors had a higher observed conversion rate than returning visitors (24.91% versus 13.93%), despite spending less time browsing product-related pages on average (10.61 versus 21.49 minutes).

Purchase conversion rates generally increased with browsing duration for both visitor types, although the difference between their conversion rates varied across duration groups. These findings motivate further investigation of the interaction between browsing duration and visitor type.

These descriptive findings are unadjusted and should not be interpreted as causal relationships.

### 8.4 Technical Appendix

#### 8.4.1 Dataset and Study Population

This study uses the Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention Dataset from the UCI Machine Learning Repository (Sakar & Kastro, 2018). The original dataset contains 12,330 browsing sessions and 18 variables, including browsing behavior, visitor characteristics, session attributes, and purchase outcomes.

The unit of analysis is an individual browsing session. The outcome variable, Revenue, indicates whether a session resulted in a purchase. The primary explanatory variables are product browsing duration and visitor type.

The analytical population was restricted to new and returning visitors, resulting in a final sample of 12,245 sessions.

#### 8.4.2 Data Cleaning and Exclusions

No missing values were identified in the original dataset. A total of 125 duplicate records were detected and provisionally retained because unique session identifiers were unavailable.

Additionally, 755 sessions had zero recorded product browsing duration, and 961 observations were identified as potential outliers using the 1.5 × IQR rule. No observations were removed solely based on these characteristics because they did not necessarily indicate data errors.

The Other visitor category was excluded because it fell outside the scope of the research question. This removed 85 observations, retaining 99.31% of the original dataset.

Categorical predictors were converted into factors, with new visitors serving as the reference category for visitor type. The purchase outcome was recoded as 0 for no purchase and 1 for purchase.

#### 8.4.3 Variable Transformation

Product browsing duration was converted from seconds to minutes to facilitate interpretation. In the original dataset, the duration distribution was highly right-skewed, with a skewness of 7.262.

A log(1 + x) transformation reduced skewness to −0.076 while preserving zero-duration observations. Both untransformed and transformed durations were retained for subsequent model development.

The final functional form should be determined based on model specification and diagnostic assessment rather than predictor normality alone.

## 9 References

Holst, C. (2025, February 2). *Reasons for cart abandonment – Why 70% of users abandon their cart*. Baymard Institute. <https://baymard.com/research-articles/ecommerce-checkout-usability-report-and-benchmark>

Sakar, C. O., & Kastro, Y. (2018). *Online shoppers purchasing intention dataset* \[Data set\]. UCI Machine Learning Repository. <https://doi.org/10.24432/C5F88Q>

Sakar, C. O., Polat, S. O., Katircioglu, M., & Kastro, Y. (2019). Real-time prediction of online shoppers’ purchasing intention using multilayer perceptron and LSTM recurrent neural networks. *Neural Computing and Applications, 31*, 6893–6908. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s00521-018-3523-0>

# B. Statistical Modeling & Inference

## 1. Model Formulation

Multiple logistic regression was selected because the outcome of interest is binary: a shopper either makes a purchase or does not. This model allows us to examine the association between product browsing duration and purchase likelihood while controlling for other browsing behaviors and session characteristics.

We will fit two models: a main effects model and an interaction model. The interaction model allows us to assess whether the association between product browsing duration and purchase likelihood differs between new and returning visitors.

### Model 1: Main Effects Model

$$Y_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p_i)$$

$$\log\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right)
= \beta_0 + \beta_1D_i + \beta_2V_i
+ \beta_3P_i + \beta_4W_i$$

### Model 2: Interaction Model

$$\log\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right)
= \beta_0 + \beta_1D_i + \beta_2V_i
+ \beta_3P_i + \beta_4W_i
+ \beta_5(D_i \times V_i)$$

Where:

| Symbol | Description |
|--------------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| $Y_i$ | Purchase outcome (1 = purchase, 0 = no purchase) |
| $p_i$ | Probability of purchase for session $i$ |
| $D_i$ | Product browsing duration (minutes) |
| $V_i$ | Visitor type (0 = new, 1 = returning) |
| $P_i$ | Number of product-related pages visited |
| $W_i$ | Weekend status (0 = weekday, 1 = weekend) |
| $D_i \times V_i$ | Interaction between browsing duration and visitor type |
| $\beta_0$ | Intercept |
| $\beta_1, \ldots, \beta_5$ | Regression coefficients |

## 2. Covariate Selection

Covariates were selected based on the research question, subject-matter relevance, and exploratory data analysis.

Product browsing duration and visitor type (new or returning) were selected as the primary independent variables. An interaction term between these variables will be included to assess whether the association between browsing duration and purchase likelihood differs by visitor type.

The following variables were selected as initial controls:

- **Number of product-related pages visited:** Accounts for the volume of product browsing, allowing us to examine the association between browsing duration and purchase likelihood while holding page count constant.

- **Weekend status:** Accounts for potential differences in shopping behavior between weekdays and weekends.

Exploratory data analysis revealed a strong correlation between product page count and browsing duration ($r = 0.861$). Both variables will initially be retained because of their relevance to the research question. Potential multicollinearity will be further assessed using variance inflation factors (VIF).

Additional browsing behaviors and session characteristics will be considered as potential covariates during model assessment. Page value will be excluded due to its potential to incorporate information related to the purchase outcome.

## 3. Multiple Logistic Regression

We first fit a multiple logistic regression model without an interaction term to establish a baseline for comparison. This model estimates the association between product browsing duration and purchase likelihood while accounting for visitor type, product page count, and weekend status.

```{r}
# Fit main effects logistic regression model
model1 <- glm(
  Revenue ~ Duration_Minutes + VisitorType + ProductRelated + Weekend,
  data = df_clean,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)

# Display model summary
summary(model1)
```

### 3.1. Coefficient Estimates

All four predictors were statistically significant at the 0.05 significance level. Since logistic regression coefficients are estimated on the log-odds scale, we exponentiate the coefficients to obtain odds ratios for more intuitive interpretation.

$$OR_j = e^{\hat{\beta}_j}$$

```{r}
library(broom)

# Calculate odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals
model1_results <- tidy(
  model1,
  conf.int = TRUE,
  conf.level = 0.95,
  exponentiate = TRUE
)

model1_results
```

### 3.2. Interpretation of Results

Holding all other predictors constant:

- **Product browsing duration:** Each additional minute spent browsing product-related pages is associated with a 0.55% increase in the odds of purchasing ($OR = 1.0055$, $p < 0.001$).

- **Visitor type:** Returning visitors have approximately 59.4% lower odds of purchasing compared to new visitors ($OR = 0.4059$, $p < 0.001$).

- **Product page count:** Each additional product-related page visited is associated with a 0.53% increase in the odds of purchasing ($OR = 1.0053$, $p < 0.001$).

- **Weekend status:** Visitors browsing on weekends have approximately 15.9% higher odds of purchasing compared to visitors browsing on weekdays ($OR = 1.1594$, $p = 0.0116$).

These results suggest that both the duration and volume of product browsing are positively associated with the odds of purchasing. Returning visitors have substantially lower estimated odds of purchasing than new visitors, even after accounting for browsing duration, product page count, and weekend status.

### 3.3. Preliminary Model Assessment

The main effects model was fitted using 12,245 browsing sessions and successfully converged after four iterations.

| Metric            |  Value |
|-------------------|-------:|
| Sample size       | 12,245 |
| Null deviance     | 10,542 |
| Residual deviance | 10,101 |
| AIC               | 10,111 |

The reduction from the null deviance to the residual deviance indicates that the inclusion of the predictors improves model fit relative to an intercept-only model.

However, the main effects model assumes that the association between product browsing duration and the log odds of purchasing is the same for new and returning visitors. To directly address our research question, we will extend this model by introducing an interaction term between browsing duration and visitor type.

Further assessment of model assumptions and performance will be conducted in the model diagnostics section.

## 4. Logistic Regression with Interaction

### 4.1. Model Estimation

To directly address our research question, we extend the main effects model by including an interaction term between product browsing duration and visitor type. This allows the association between browsing duration and the log odds of purchasing to differ between new and returning visitors, while controlling for product page count and weekend status.

```{r}
# Fit logistic regression model with interaction
model2 <- glm(
  Revenue ~ Duration_Minutes * VisitorType + ProductRelated + Weekend,
  data = df_clean,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)

# Display model summary
summary(model2)
```

### 4.2. Coefficient Estimates

All predictors, including the interaction term between product browsing duration and visitor type, were statistically significant at the 0.05 significance level.

```{r}
# Calculate odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals
model2_results <- tidy(
  model2,
  conf.int = TRUE,
  conf.level = 0.95,
  exponentiate = TRUE
)

model2_results
```

### 4.3. Interpretation of Interaction Effect

The interaction between product browsing duration and returning visitor status was negative and statistically significant ($\hat{\beta}_5 = -0.020527$, $p < 0.001$). This provides evidence that the association between product browsing duration and the log odds of purchasing differs between new and returning visitors.

For new visitors, the estimated change in log odds for each additional minute of product browsing is:

$$\hat{\beta}_1 = 0.025137$$

For returning visitors, the estimated change in log odds for each additional minute of product browsing is:

$$\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_5
= 0.025137 - 0.020527
= 0.004610$$

```{r}
# Extract duration and interaction coefficients
beta_duration <- coef(model2)["Duration_Minutes"]

beta_interaction <- coef(model2)[
  "Duration_Minutes:VisitorTypeReturning_Visitor"
]

# Calculate visitor-specific odds ratios
or_new <- exp(beta_duration)
or_returning <- exp(beta_duration + beta_interaction)

# Summarize visitor-specific effects
visitor_effects <- tibble(
  `Visitor Type` = c("New Visitor", "Returning Visitor"),
  `Log-Odds Coefficient` = c(
    beta_duration,
    beta_duration + beta_interaction
  ),
  `Odds Ratio` = c(or_new, or_returning),
  `Percent Change in Odds` = c(
    (or_new - 1) * 100,
    (or_returning - 1) * 100
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  visitor_effects,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Estimated association between browsing duration
  and purchase odds by visitor type."
)
```

Holding product page count and weekend status constant:

- **New visitors:** Each additional minute spent browsing product-related pages is associated with approximately 2.55% higher odds of purchasing.

- **Returning visitors:** Each additional minute spent browsing product-related pages is associated with approximately 0.46% higher odds of purchasing.

- **Interaction effect:** The negative interaction coefficient indicates that the positive association between browsing duration and purchase odds is weaker for returning visitors than for new visitors.

These findings suggest that visitor type moderates the relationship between product browsing duration and purchase odds. However, these results describe statistical associations rather than causal relationships.

### 4.4. Preliminary Model Assessment

The interaction model was fitted using 12,245 browsing sessions and successfully converged after four iterations.

| Metric            |  Value |
|-------------------|-------:|
| Sample size       | 12,245 |
| Null deviance     | 10,542 |
| Residual deviance | 10,080 |
| AIC               | 10,092 |

Compared with the main effects model, the interaction model has a lower residual deviance and AIC, providing preliminary evidence of improved model fit.

A formal likelihood ratio test will be conducted to determine whether including the interaction term significantly improves model fit.

## 5. Model Comparison

The main effects model and interaction model were compared using a likelihood ratio test and Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) to determine whether including the interaction term improves model fit.

### 5.1. Likelihood Ratio Test

Because the main effects model is nested within the interaction model, a likelihood ratio test can be used to assess whether the additional interaction term significantly improves model fit.

The hypotheses are:

$$H_0: \beta_5 = 0$$

$$H_A: \beta_5 \neq 0$$

Under the null hypothesis, the association between product browsing duration and the log odds of purchasing does not differ between new and returning visitors.

The test statistic is calculated as:

$$\Lambda = 2[\ell(M_2) - \ell(M_1)]$$

where $\ell(M_1)$ and $\ell(M_2)$ represent the log-likelihoods of the main effects and interaction models, respectively. Under the null hypothesis, the test statistic approximately follows a chi-square distribution with one degree of freedom.

```{r}
# Compare nested models using a likelihood ratio test
anova(model1, model2, test = "Chisq")
```

### 5.2. AIC Comparison

Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) was used to compare the two models while accounting for differences in model complexity. A lower AIC indicates a more favorable balance between model fit and complexity.

```{r}
# Compare model fit statistics
model_comparison <- tibble(
  Model = c("Main Effects Model", "Interaction Model"),
  Parameters = c(
    length(coef(model1)),
    length(coef(model2))
  ),
  `Residual Deviance` = c(
    deviance(model1),
    deviance(model2)
  ),
  AIC = c(AIC(model1), AIC(model2))
)

knitr::kable(
  model_comparison,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Comparison of logistic regression models."
)
```

The interaction model has a lower AIC than the main effects model, suggesting that the improvement in model fit outweighs the penalty for including an additional parameter.

### 5.3. Model Selection

The likelihood ratio test indicated that the interaction model provided a statistically significant improvement in fit compared to the main effects model ($\chi^2(1) = 20.688$, $p < 0.001$). Therefore, we reject the null hypothesis that the interaction coefficient is equal to zero.

The interaction model also had a lower AIC (10,092.25) than the main effects model (10,110.94), representing a reduction of 18.69. This suggests that the improvement in model fit outweighs the penalty for including an additional parameter.

Based on both the likelihood ratio test and AIC comparison, the interaction model was selected as the preferred model for subsequent statistical inference and interpretation.

These results provide evidence that the association between product browsing duration and the log odds of purchasing differs between new and returning visitors, after accounting for product page count and weekend status.

The selected model will undergo further diagnostic assessment to evaluate model assumptions and performance.

## 6. Statistical Inference and Interpretation

### 6.1. Regression Results

Regression coefficients were exponentiated to obtain odds ratios, allowing for more intuitive interpretation of the association between each predictor and purchase odds. Standard errors on the odds-ratio scale were approximated using the delta method. We report 95% confidence intervals and p-values to assess statistical uncertainty.

```{r}
# Function to format logistic regression results
format_results <- function(model) {
  broom::tidy(
    model,
    conf.int = TRUE,
    conf.level = 0.95,
    exponentiate = TRUE
  ) %>%
    mutate(
      std.error = estimate * std.error,
      term = recode(
        term,
        "(Intercept)" = "Intercept",
        "Duration_Minutes" = "Product browsing duration (min)",
        "VisitorTypeReturning_Visitor" = "Returning visitor",
        "ProductRelated" = "Product page count",
        "WeekendTRUE" = "Weekend",
        "Duration_Minutes:VisitorTypeReturning_Visitor" =
          "Browsing duration × Returning visitor"
      )
    ) %>%
    transmute(
      Predictor = term,
      `Odds Ratio` = round(estimate, 4),
      `Standard Error` = round(std.error, 4),
      `95% CI Lower` = round(conf.low, 4),
      `95% CI Upper` = round(conf.high, 4),
      `P-value` = ifelse(
        p.value < 0.001,
        "<0.001",
        sprintf("%.4f", p.value)
      )
    )
}

# Generate formatted results for both models
model1_table <- format_results(model1)
model2_table <- format_results(model2)

knitr::kable(
  model1_table,
  caption = "Model 1: Main effects logistic regression."
)

knitr::kable(
  model2_table,
  caption = "Model 2: Logistic regression with interaction."
)
```

### 6.2. Visitor-Specific Effects

To further investigate the interaction between product browsing duration and visitor type, we estimated visitor-specific odds ratios, 95% confidence intervals, and p-values.

For new visitors, the duration coefficient is $\hat{\beta}_1$. For returning visitors, the duration coefficient is $\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_5$.

The standard error of the combined coefficient accounts for both the variances and covariance of the estimated coefficients.

```{r}
# Extract coefficients and variance-covariance matrix
b <- coef(model2)
V <- vcov(model2)

duration_term <- "Duration_Minutes"
interaction_term <- "Duration_Minutes:VisitorTypeReturning_Visitor"

# New visitors
beta_new <- b[duration_term]
se_new <- sqrt(V[duration_term, duration_term])

# Returning visitors
beta_returning <- b[duration_term] + b[interaction_term]

se_returning <- sqrt(
  V[duration_term, duration_term] +
  V[interaction_term, interaction_term] +
  2 * V[duration_term, interaction_term]
)

# Calculate visitor-specific inference statistics
visitor_inference <- tibble(
  Visitor = c("New Visitor", "Returning Visitor"),
  beta = c(beta_new, beta_returning),
  se = c(se_new, se_returning)
) %>%
  mutate(
    odds_ratio = exp(beta),
    ci_lower = exp(beta - qnorm(0.975) * se),
    ci_upper = exp(beta + qnorm(0.975) * se),
    p_value = 2 * pnorm(-abs(beta / se)),
    percent_change = (odds_ratio - 1) * 100
  )

# Format results
visitor_inference_table <- visitor_inference %>%
  transmute(
    `Visitor Type` = Visitor,
    `Odds Ratio` = round(odds_ratio, 4),
    `95% CI Lower` = round(ci_lower, 4),
    `95% CI Upper` = round(ci_upper, 4),
    `Change in Odds (%)` = round(percent_change, 2),
    `P-value` = ifelse(
      p_value < 0.001,
      "<0.001",
      sprintf("%.4f", p_value)
    )
  )

knitr::kable(
  visitor_inference_table,
  caption = "Visitor-specific associations between product
  browsing duration and purchase odds."
)
```

### 6.3. Summary of Findings

Product browsing duration was positively and statistically significantly associated with purchase odds for both new and returning visitors, after accounting for product page count and weekend status.

For new visitors, each additional minute spent browsing product-related pages was associated with a 2.55% increase in the odds of purchasing (OR = 1.0255, 95% CI: 1.0161–1.0349, p \< 0.001).

For returning visitors, each additional minute was associated with a 0.46% increase in the odds of purchasing (OR = 1.0046, 95% CI: 1.0016–1.0077, p = 0.0029).

The statistically significant negative interaction coefficient indicates that the positive association between product browsing duration and purchase odds is stronger for new visitors than for returning visitors.

These findings suggest that product browsing duration may be a more informative indicator of purchase intent among new visitors. However, the observational nature of the data prevents us from establishing a causal relationship between browsing duration and purchasing behavior.

These conclusions remain subject to further assessment of model assumptions and adequacy.

## 7. Predicted Purchase Probabilities

### 7.1. Generate Predicted Probabilities

To visualize the interaction between product browsing duration and visitor type, predicted purchase probabilities were calculated using the selected interaction model.

Product page count was held constant at its median value of 18 pages. The median was selected because the distribution of product page count is right-skewed, making it less sensitive to extreme observations than the mean. Weekend status was held constant at weekday.

Holding these variables constant allows us to isolate the modeled association between browsing duration and purchase probability across visitor types. Browsing duration was varied from zero to its 95th percentile to focus on the range containing most observed sessions.

```{r}
# Define range of browsing duration
duration_range <- seq(
  from = 0,
  to = quantile(df_clean$Duration_Minutes, 0.95),
  length.out = 200
)

# Create prediction dataset
prediction_data <- expand.grid(
  Duration_Minutes = duration_range,
  VisitorType = levels(df_clean$VisitorType),
  ProductRelated = median(df_clean$ProductRelated),
  Weekend = "FALSE"
)

# Match factor levels to original dataset
prediction_data$VisitorType <- factor(
  prediction_data$VisitorType,
  levels = levels(df_clean$VisitorType)
)

prediction_data$Weekend <- factor(
  prediction_data$Weekend,
  levels = levels(df_clean$Weekend)
)

# Generate predictions on the log-odds scale
predictions <- predict(
  model2,
  newdata = prediction_data,
  type = "link",
  se.fit = TRUE
)

# Convert log odds to probabilities
prediction_data <- prediction_data %>%
  mutate(
    probability = plogis(predictions$fit),
    ci_lower = plogis(
      predictions$fit - qnorm(0.975) * predictions$se.fit
    ),
    ci_upper = plogis(
      predictions$fit + qnorm(0.975) * predictions$se.fit
    ),
    Visitor = recode(
      VisitorType,
      "New_Visitor" = "New Visitor",
      "Returning_Visitor" = "Returning Visitor"
    )
  )
```

### 7.2. Visualize Predicted Purchase Probabilities

Predicted purchase probabilities were plotted against product browsing duration for each visitor type. Shaded regions represent pointwise 95% confidence intervals for the estimated probabilities.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

ggplot(
  prediction_data,
  aes(
    x = Duration_Minutes,
    y = probability,
    color = Visitor,
    fill = Visitor
  )
) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(ymin = ci_lower, ymax = ci_upper),
    alpha = 0.15,
    color = NA
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "New Visitor" = "#2563EB",
      "Returning Visitor" = "#D97706"
    )
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "New Visitor" = "#2563EB",
      "Returning Visitor" = "#D97706"
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_percent()
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted Purchase Probability by Visitor Type",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Weekday sessions with ",
      median(df_clean$ProductRelated),
      " product pages visited"
    ),
    x = "Product Browsing Duration (Minutes)",
    y = "Predicted Purchase Probability",
    color = NULL,
    fill = NULL,
    caption = "Shaded regions represent pointwise 95% confidence intervals."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )


```

### 7.3. Interpretation of Predicted Probabilities

The predicted probability curves illustrate the interaction
between product browsing duration and visitor type. While
predicted purchase probability increases with browsing
duration for both visitor groups, the increase is
substantially greater for new visitors.

To ensure a consistent comparison between visitor types,
product page count was held constant at its median value
of 18 pages, and weekend status was held constant at weekday.

Under these conditions, as product browsing duration
increases from 20 to 60 minutes, the predicted purchase
probability for new visitors increases from approximately
28% to 52%. In comparison, the predicted purchase
probability for returning visitors increases from
approximately 12% to 14%.

The widening gap between the two curves is consistent
with the statistically significant interaction identified
in the regression model. The confidence intervals also
widen at longer browsing durations, particularly for new
visitors, indicating greater uncertainty in the estimated
probabilities.

From a business perspective, these findings suggest that
product browsing duration may be a more informative
indicator of purchase intent among new visitors than
returning visitors.

However, these predictions are conditional on the selected
control variable values and do not represent average
purchase probabilities across all visitors. Given the
strong correlation between product page count and browsing
duration, predictions at longer durations should be
interpreted with caution until the observed data support
for these combinations has been assessed. Additionally,
the observed associations should not be interpreted as
causal relationships.
